questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A security team is replacing per-user IAM policies with a model that can scale across hundreds of engineers and workloads. What design should be used?

answers.text: Define job-function roles and group assignments, then attach managed policies that represent approved permission sets
Attach a unique inline policy to every individual user
Share one administrator user across all engineers
Use security group membership as the AWS permission model

explanations.a: Group-based and role-based assignments reduce per-user policy sprawl and make authorization changes easier to review and audit.
explanations.b: Individual inline policies are difficult to review and do not scale across many engineers.
explanations.c: Shared users remove individual accountability and overgrant access.
explanations.d: Security groups control network traffic and do not assign IAM permissions to humans.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A company has development, staging, and production accounts. Developers need read access to production and write access to development. What authorization model fits?

answers.text: One role with AdministratorAccess in every account
Separate roles or permission sets by environment with group-based assignment
One IAM user per environment with shared passwords
Resource tags only, with no IAM policies

explanations.a: A single broad role ignores environment risk differences and violates least privilege.
explanations.b: Environment-specific roles allow permissions to reflect risk and job need without granting broad access everywhere.
explanations.c: Shared users weaken accountability and credential lifecycle control.
explanations.d: Tags can support authorization, but policies must still enforce the decisions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A security architect wants application teams to create roles only from approved permission patterns. What scalable model helps?

answers.text: Unreviewed inline policies written manually in the console
A policy that grants iam:* to every team role
Reusable managed policies and permission boundaries applied through infrastructure as code
An email thread listing allowed actions

explanations.a: Manual inline policies can drift and are hard to govern at scale.
explanations.b: Broad IAM access can enable privilege escalation.
explanations.c: Managed patterns and boundaries let teams self-serve while staying inside approved authorization limits.
explanations.d: Email guidance does not enforce authorization controls.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A company needs a central way to provide read-only, billing, and security-audit access across many accounts. What should be created?

answers.text: Separate unmanaged IAM users in each account for every employee
One account root user login for auditors
Bucket ACLs that list every auditor
Standardized roles or IAM Identity Center permission sets assigned to appropriate groups

explanations.a: Per-account users make deprovisioning and audit harder.
explanations.b: Root access is excessive and cannot represent multiple auditors safely.
explanations.c: Bucket ACLs do not grant broad account audit permissions.
explanations.d: Standard permission sets keep access consistent across accounts while still mapping to different job functions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A startup has grown quickly, and many policies contain wildcards because teams copied old examples. What is the best scalable improvement?

answers.text: Create reviewed policy templates for common job functions and migrate teams to those templates
Keep copying old wildcard policies because they are already working
Delete all policies before understanding dependencies
Allow every team to create administrator roles to avoid policy review

explanations.a: Reviewed templates reduce copy-paste permission drift and create a consistent baseline for future access changes.
explanations.b: Working access can still be excessive and risky.
explanations.c: Unscoped deletion can break production workloads.
explanations.d: Administrator roles increase blast radius and defeat the scalable model.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A workload needs separate permissions for deployment, runtime, and break-glass operations. What model is appropriate?

answers.text: Use one role for deployment, runtime, and emergency actions
Use distinct roles for each operational context with different trust policies and permissions
Use local application configuration files as the IAM authority
Use only resource names to imply permission level

explanations.a: One role combines unrelated privileges and expands impact if compromised.
explanations.b: Separating roles by context limits what each activity can do and improves audit clarity.
explanations.c: Local files do not control AWS authorization decisions.
explanations.d: Naming conventions do not enforce IAM access.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A company wants to grant access based on project membership and environment but avoid creating thousands of project-specific policies. What model should be considered?

answers.text: Create one administrator policy per project and attach it broadly
Let users self-assign any project tag without controls
ABAC with governed principal tags and resource tags
Use VPC route tables to determine project permissions

explanations.a: Project-specific administrator policies overgrant and do not reduce risk.
explanations.b: ABAC depends on trusted attributes, so tag assignment must be governed.
explanations.c: Attribute-based access control can scale project authorization by comparing trusted attributes rather than creating a policy per project.
explanations.d: Route tables control network paths and do not grant API authorization.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.1: Design and implement a scalable authorization model that includes users, groups, roles, and policies.
questions.text: A security review finds roles with similar names but different permissions across accounts. What should the authorization model do?

answers.text: Rely on name similarity as proof of identical access
Require analysts to inspect every role manually every day
Remove all role names and keep only policy documents
Standardize role definitions and policy versions through centralized IaC and account baselines

explanations.a: Similar names do not guarantee the same permissions.
explanations.b: Daily manual inspection is not scalable across many accounts.
explanations.c: Missing names make ownership and operational use harder.
explanations.d: Consistent role definitions reduce confusion and make cross-account access review more reliable.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A company uses an external identity provider and wants employees to access AWS accounts without IAM users. What should be implemented?

answers.text: IAM Identity Center integrated with the external identity provider
A shared IAM user for each department
Long-term access keys for every employee
Security groups mapped to corporate groups

explanations.a: IAM Identity Center provides federated workforce access to multiple accounts without creating separate IAM users.
explanations.b: Shared users weaken individual accountability and do not use the external identity lifecycle.
explanations.c: Long-term keys increase rotation burden and are not ideal for workforce console access.
explanations.d: Security groups are network controls and do not provide workforce federation.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A SAML federation setup allows users into the wrong AWS role. What should be checked?

answers.text: Only the EC2 instance type in the account
Identity provider group mappings, SAML attributes, role trust policy, and permission set assignment
Only the S3 bucket storage class
Only CloudFront response headers

explanations.a: Instance type does not control SAML role mapping.
explanations.b: Federation depends on both identity-provider assertions and AWS-side role or permission set configuration.
explanations.c: Storage class does not assign federated roles.
explanations.d: Response headers do not determine SAML role assumption.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A contractor should lose AWS access immediately when removed from a corporate directory group. Which design supports this?

answers.text: Standalone IAM users created for each contractor
A shared role password for all contractors
Group-based federated access through the identity provider
A resource tag that says contractor

explanations.a: Standalone users can remain active after directory removal if not separately disabled.
explanations.b: Shared passwords cannot be tied to individual employment status.
explanations.c: Federated group membership connects AWS access to the central identity lifecycle.
explanations.d: Tags do not automatically authenticate or deprovision workforce users.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A company wants MFA enforcement for privileged AWS console roles. Where should this primarily be enforced for federated users?

answers.text: Only in application source code comments
By storing one MFA code in Secrets Manager
By disabling federation and using root logins
At the identity provider and permission assignment process, with AWS conditions where applicable

explanations.a: Comments do not enforce MFA.
explanations.b: MFA codes should not be shared or stored as static secrets.
explanations.c: Root logins are not an appropriate workforce access model.
explanations.d: Federated access usually receives MFA context from the identity provider, and privileged assignments should require strong authentication.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A user can access an AWS account after being removed from the expected group. What should be investigated?

answers.text: SCIM provisioning status, group assignments, permission set assignments, and active sessions
Only the user's preferred AWS Region
Only the cost allocation tags on resources
Only the VPC CIDR block

explanations.a: Federated deprovisioning issues can come from identity synchronization, stale assignments, or still-valid sessions.
explanations.b: Preferred Region does not grant account access.
explanations.c: Cost tags do not control workforce federation.
explanations.d: Network addressing does not explain federated account assignment.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A company needs temporary CLI access through its workforce identity provider. What access pattern fits?

answers.text: Create permanent IAM access keys for every user
Federated role sessions or IAM Identity Center credential vending for assigned permission sets
Email the root access key during emergencies
Use an S3 presigned URL as the AWS CLI identity

explanations.a: Permanent keys bypass the workforce session model and increase credential exposure.
explanations.b: Temporary federated sessions avoid permanent user keys while supporting CLI access.
explanations.c: Root keys should not be distributed to workforce users.
explanations.d: Presigned URLs authorize object access and do not authenticate the AWS CLI broadly.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A security team wants CloudTrail events to show who performed actions after federation. What should be configured?

answers.text: One shared federated session name for all users
Disable CloudTrail to reduce identity data
Identifiable federated session names and consistent identity attributes
Use random names with no user mapping

explanations.a: Shared session names make attribution difficult.
explanations.b: Disabling audit logs removes evidence of federated activity.
explanations.c: Auditability requires session context that links AWS actions back to the workforce identity.
explanations.d: Random unmapped sessions weaken investigation and access review.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.2: Design and implement identity federation for workforce access.
questions.text: A federation trust policy is too broad and permits role assumption from any SAML provider in the account. What should be tightened?

answers.text: Add AdministratorAccess to every federated session
Remove all conditions from the trust policy
Move the role to a public subnet
Restrict the trust policy to the approved provider and required audience or attribute conditions

explanations.a: More permissions do not fix an overly broad trust relationship.
explanations.b: Removing conditions further broadens who can assume the role.
explanations.c: Network placement does not constrain SAML trust.
explanations.d: Federation trust should accept assertions only from intended providers and contexts.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: An application running on EC2 needs to call DynamoDB. Which authentication approach is preferred?

answers.text: Use an instance profile with an IAM role that grants the required DynamoDB actions
Store an IAM access key in the AMI
Use the account root credentials in an environment variable
Use an IAM group attached to the instance

explanations.a: Instance profiles provide temporary credentials to EC2 workloads without embedding static keys.
explanations.b: AMI-baked keys spread long-term credentials to every instance created from the image.
explanations.c: Root credentials are excessive and unsafe for workload authentication.
explanations.d: IAM groups are for users and cannot be attached to EC2 instances.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: An ECS task should access one SQS queue. Other tasks on the same host must not inherit this access. What should be used?

answers.text: The container instance role for all tasks
An ECS task role scoped to the SQS queue
A plaintext access key in the container image
A security group rule that grants SQS permissions

explanations.a: The instance role can overgrant every task running on the host.
explanations.b: Task roles provide per-task temporary credentials and prevent sharing host-level permissions with unrelated tasks.
explanations.c: Image-embedded keys are long-term credentials and can leak to anyone with image access.
explanations.d: Security groups do not authorize SQS API calls.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: An EKS pod needs AWS permissions independent of the node role. Which pattern should be implemented?

answers.text: Share the node instance profile with every pod
Put access keys in a Kubernetes ConfigMap
IAM roles for service accounts
Authorize the pod by its container image name only

explanations.a: Node-level credentials can overgrant workloads and weaken isolation.
explanations.b: ConfigMaps are not appropriate for long-term AWS credentials.
explanations.c: IAM roles for service accounts give pods scoped temporary AWS credentials tied to Kubernetes service accounts.
explanations.d: Image names do not grant AWS API permissions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: A Lambda function must decrypt a secret and publish logs. What should authorize those actions?

answers.text: A human console password stored in the function package
A bucket ACL on the deployment artifact
An IAM group assigned to the function
The Lambda execution role with scoped KMS, Secrets Manager, and CloudWatch Logs permissions

explanations.a: Human passwords should not be packaged with application code.
explanations.b: Artifact ACLs do not grant runtime KMS or log permissions.
explanations.c: IAM groups are not attached to Lambda functions.
explanations.d: Lambda uses its execution role for AWS API calls during function execution.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: A third-party CI system outside AWS needs to deploy to an AWS account without long-term keys. Which authentication method fits?

answers.text: OIDC federation to assume a deployment role with scoped permissions
A permanent administrator access key stored in the CI system
A shared root password stored in the CI project
Public write access to deployment resources

explanations.a: OIDC-based role assumption gives the external workload temporary credentials tied to trusted token claims.
explanations.b: Long-term administrator keys increase exposure and rotation burden.
explanations.c: Root credentials must not be stored in external automation.
explanations.d: Public access is not a secure authentication method.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: An application uses STS AssumeRole for tenant-specific operations. What should be controlled?

answers.text: Allow every tenant to assume every tenant role
Trust policy conditions, session duration, session tags, and allowed role permissions
Use unlimited session duration for all tenant operations
Ignore session tags because they are never used in authorization

explanations.a: Unrestricted tenant role assumption breaks isolation.
explanations.b: Assumed-role sessions need bounded trust, time, attributes, and permissions to prevent cross-tenant misuse.
explanations.c: Long sessions increase exposure if credentials are compromised.
explanations.d: Session tags can affect ABAC and audit context when policies use them.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: A workload running in another AWS account needs access to an S3 bucket. What authentication and authorization path should be used?

answers.text: Copy a user access key from the bucket account into the workload account
Make the bucket public to avoid cross-account permissions
Assume a cross-account role or use a resource policy that trusts the workload role and scopes access
Use a VPC subnet tag as the only trust mechanism

explanations.a: Shared long-term keys weaken accountability and are hard to rotate.
explanations.b: Public access exposes data beyond the intended workload.
explanations.c: Cross-account workload access requires an explicit trust path and least-privilege permissions on the target resource.
explanations.d: Subnet tags do not authenticate AWS principals.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.3: Design and implement application and workload authentication by using IAM roles and temporary credentials.
questions.text: A workload cannot refresh temporary credentials and fails after several hours. What should be reviewed?

answers.text: Only the application logo file
Only the S3 lifecycle policy for logs
Only the number of IAM users in the account
Credential provider chain, runtime role attachment, session duration, and application credential caching

explanations.a: Static assets do not control credential refresh.
explanations.b: Log lifecycle does not explain expired runtime credentials.
explanations.c: User count does not show how the workload refreshes credentials.
explanations.d: Temporary credential authentication depends on the runtime obtaining and refreshing credentials correctly.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: A security account must read CloudTrail logs in workload accounts. What cross-account access pattern is appropriate?

answers.text: A role in each workload account that trusts the security account and grants read-only log access
Share root credentials from every workload account
Make all audit logs public
Copy logs manually through personal email

explanations.a: Cross-account roles provide auditable, temporary access to specific resources in member accounts.
explanations.b: Root credential sharing is excessive and unsafe.
explanations.c: Public logs can expose sensitive account activity.
explanations.d: Manual email transfer is incomplete and hard to audit.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: A cross-account role assumption fails with AccessDenied. What must be present?

answers.text: Only an S3 bucket in the source account
Caller permission to assume the role and a target role trust policy that allows the caller
Only matching account aliases
Only a public subnet route

explanations.a: A bucket does not authorize STS role assumption.
explanations.b: Cross-account access requires both identity-side permission and target-side trust.
explanations.c: Aliases do not create trust relationships.
explanations.d: Network routes do not grant IAM trust.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: A vendor needs access to one AWS account to collect metrics. Which trust control reduces confused-deputy risk?

answers.text: Trust every AWS account root principal
Use the role name as a secret
Require an external ID in the cross-account role trust policy
Remove all trust policy conditions

explanations.a: Broad trust increases unauthorized assumption risk.
explanations.b: Role names are not reliable secrets.
explanations.c: External IDs help ensure the vendor assumes the role only for the intended customer context.
explanations.d: Removing conditions weakens third-party trust controls.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: An operations role in a central account can assume roles in production and development. Production should require stronger controls. What should be configured?

answers.text: Use identical unrestricted roles in every account
Allow production access only through shared access keys
Disable CloudTrail for production assumptions
Separate production trust conditions, permission scope, session duration, and approval or MFA requirements

explanations.a: Uniform unrestricted roles ignore production risk.
explanations.b: Shared keys reduce attribution and violate temporary access patterns.
explanations.c: Privileged production access needs audit evidence.
explanations.d: Higher-risk accounts need tighter assumption conditions and shorter, more governed sessions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: An IAM role in Account A must access an S3 bucket in Account B. Access still fails after the role policy allows s3:GetObject. What might be missing?

answers.text: A bucket policy or ownership configuration that permits the role from Account A
An EC2 security group rule in Account A
A longer role session name
CloudFront caching in Account B

explanations.a: Cross-account S3 access commonly requires both identity permission and resource-side permission or ownership alignment.
explanations.b: Security groups do not authorize S3 object access.
explanations.c: Session name length does not grant bucket permissions.
explanations.d: CloudFront caching does not authorize direct S3 GetObject requests.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: A central automation role uses Organizations to deploy guardrails. What should limit its cross-account power?

answers.text: Unrestricted administrator access with no logging
Least-privilege target roles, explicit trust, and monitored organization-level actions
Root credentials stored in the automation repository
Public trust policies so any account can invoke the automation

explanations.a: Broad unmonitored access creates organization-wide risk.
explanations.b: Central automation needs enough authority to deploy controls but should be scoped and auditable.
explanations.c: Root credentials should not be stored in code.
explanations.d: Public trust would allow unintended principals to act.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: A cross-account role uses session tags for project scoping. What must the trust policy control?

answers.text: Let every caller set any session tag
Delete resource tags from all target resources
Which principals can pass session tags and which tag keys or values are allowed
Use tags only in role descriptions

explanations.a: Unrestricted tag setting can bypass ABAC project boundaries.
explanations.b: Removing resource tags can break tag-based access decisions.
explanations.c: Session tags can influence authorization and audit, so tag passing must be constrained.
explanations.d: Descriptions do not enforce session tag controls.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.4: Design, implement, and troubleshoot multi-account access patterns.
questions.text: A multi-account access review finds roles trusted by unknown external accounts. What should be done?

answers.text: Ignore external trust when the role has not been used recently
Rename roles to hide them from external accounts
Add more external principals for redundancy
Use IAM Access Analyzer findings and update trust policies to approved principals only

explanations.a: Unused external trust can still be abused later.
explanations.b: Renaming does not remove trust relationships.
explanations.c: More trust expands exposure rather than remediating it.
explanations.d: Access Analyzer can identify external access paths, and trust policies should be constrained to intended accounts.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A company wants central workforce access management across AWS accounts. Which service should be used?

answers.text: IAM Identity Center with permission sets assigned to identity provider groups
Individual IAM users in every account
Shared administrator passwords
Security groups named after departments

explanations.a: IAM Identity Center centrally assigns workforce permissions across accounts using permission sets and groups.
explanations.b: Per-account IAM users make access lifecycle management difficult.
explanations.c: Shared passwords remove individual accountability.
explanations.d: Security groups do not manage workforce account access.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A security team needs to know which users have AdministratorAccess across all accounts through IAM Identity Center. What should be reviewed?

answers.text: Only VPC route tables
Permission set assignments, group membership, and account assignments
Only S3 object versions
Only CloudFront cache behaviors

explanations.a: Route tables do not determine workforce permission assignments.
explanations.b: Effective Identity Center access depends on the permission set, group mapping, and assigned accounts.
explanations.c: Object versions do not show Identity Center administration.
explanations.d: Cache behaviors do not grant account administrator access.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A user removed from an identity provider group still has an active AWS session. What governance point matters?

answers.text: Bucket lifecycle expiration
ALB idle timeout only
Session duration and revocation expectations for federated access
EBS snapshot retention

explanations.a: Object lifecycle settings do not end active workforce sessions.
explanations.b: Load balancer idle timeout does not govern AWS console role session duration.
explanations.c: Federated access can remain valid until session expiration unless the organization has a revocation process.
explanations.d: Snapshot retention does not revoke Identity Center sessions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A new AWS account is created in an organization. It should automatically receive standard security, developer, and read-only access assignments. What should be automated?

answers.text: Manual assignment whenever someone remembers
A public wiki table of who should have access
Root user sharing until assignments are created
Account vending or onboarding workflow that applies IAM Identity Center account assignments

explanations.a: Manual assignment creates inconsistent access and delays.
explanations.b: Documentation does not apply Identity Center assignments.
explanations.c: Root sharing is unsafe and not a governance bridge.
explanations.d: Identity governance should include new account onboarding so access baselines are applied consistently.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A company separates accounts into OUs for production, sandbox, and security. How should Identity Center governance reflect this?

answers.text: Use OU-aware access models and permission sets that differ by environment risk
Grant sandbox-level access to all production accounts
Use the same administrator assignment for every group in every account
Remove all group-based access and assign users manually forever

explanations.a: Different OUs often need different access levels and approval patterns because account risk varies.
explanations.b: Production needs tighter access than sandbox.
explanations.c: Universal administration ignores job function and environment risk.
explanations.d: Manual per-user assignments do not scale.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: An auditor asks who approved privileged permission set changes. What should be available?

answers.text: Only a screenshot of the final access page
Change records, assignment history, approver evidence, and CloudTrail events for Identity Center administration
Only a verbal statement from an administrator
Only EC2 instance launch logs

explanations.a: A screenshot does not prove approval or change sequence.
explanations.b: Privileged access governance needs traceability for who changed assignments and why.
explanations.c: Verbal statements are weak audit evidence.
explanations.d: Instance logs do not show Identity Center permission set governance.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A user has access through both a direct assignment and group assignment. The security team wants to simplify governance. What should be preferred?

answers.text: Many direct assignments with no owner
One shared user assigned to every permission set
Group-based assignments with direct assignments minimized and reviewed
Public access to the AWS access portal

explanations.a: Direct one-off access can become stale and difficult to audit.
explanations.b: Shared users destroy accountability.
explanations.c: Group-based assignment reduces one-off access paths and makes deprovisioning easier.
explanations.d: Public portal availability does not govern authorization assignments.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.1.5: Design and implement identity governance with IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.
questions.text: A permission set includes broad IAM administration. What governance control should apply?

answers.text: Assign it to all users for convenience
Hide the permission set from review reports
Use it as the default for new external contractors
Approval workflow, limited assignment scope, monitoring, and periodic access review

explanations.a: Broad privileged assignment increases organization-wide risk.
explanations.b: Privileged access should be more visible, not hidden.
explanations.c: Contractors should receive only approved least-privilege access.
explanations.d: Privileged permission sets require stronger governance because they can change access controls.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.1: Design and implement least-privilege access policies.
questions.text: A Lambda function needs to read one secret and write to one DynamoDB table. What policy design is best?

answers.text: Allow only secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the specific secret and required DynamoDB actions on the table
Grant AdministratorAccess because Lambda is managed
Allow secretsmanager:* on every secret
Use a network ACL rule as the permission policy

explanations.a: Least privilege scopes actions and resources to the function's actual runtime needs.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Remove CloudTrail logging for PassRole events
Store allowed role names only in comments

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Limit actions to required put operations and resources to the target bucket prefix
Make the bucket public to avoid IAM policy work

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Only the role display name
Only the number of attached policies
Only the account alias

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Limit kms:Decrypt to the required key and context where possible
Remove encryption from the secret
Use a CloudWatch dashboard title to list the key

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.1: Design and implement least-privilege access policies.

Use read-only Describe actions needed for inventory and monitoring
Share the role with all workloads

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Avoid policy review because the feature might change
Use root credentials until the feature stabilizes
Grant current required permissions and add future access through reviewed changes when needed

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Access depends only on the user's console password age

explanations.c: Encryption status does not bypass an explicit deny.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.2: Evaluate and troubleshoot IAM policy evaluation logic.

The EC2 instance state determines authorization

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.2: Evaluate and troubleshoot IAM policy evaluation logic.

Role sessions ignore all policy conditions

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.2: Evaluate and troubleshoot IAM policy evaluation logic.

The request is allowed if the API call is made from the console
The action is not allowed because the boundary limits maximum permissions

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.2: Evaluate and troubleshoot IAM policy evaluation logic.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.2: Evaluate and troubleshoot IAM policy evaluation logic.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.2: Evaluate and troubleshoot IAM policy evaluation logic.
questions.text: An access issue is hard to diagnose because identity policies, resource policies, SCPs, boundaries, and session policies all apply. What tool or approach helps?

Ignore condition keys to simplify analysis

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.
questions.text: An S3 bucket must allow read access from a role in another account. Which policy should be added to the bucket?

answers.text: A bucket policy that names the cross-account role principal and allows the required object actions
A security group rule on the bucket
An IAM group in the bucket account with no external trust
A CloudWatch alarm on bucket size

explanations.c: IAM groups do not grant a cross-account role direct S3 resource access.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.
questions.text: A Lambda function should be invokable by API Gateway but not by every AWS principal. What should be configured?

answers.text: Public invocation permission for everyone
A Lambda resource-based policy permission for the specific API Gateway source ARN
An EC2 instance profile on API Gateway
A DynamoDB table policy

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.
questions.text: A KMS key protects centralized logs. What key policy design is appropriate?

answers.text: Allow every principal in every account to decrypt
Allow application teams to delete the log archive key

Allow log delivery services and approved security roles while limiting key administration

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.
questions.text: An EventBridge event bus in a security account should receive findings from workload accounts. What policy is needed?

An S3 CORS rule on the event bus

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.

Grant access through a security group
Only tag the secret with the external account ID

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.2.3: Design and implement resource-based policies.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

questions.name: Identity and Access Management

Data lifecycle management

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.1: Design and implement service control policies and organization-level guardrails.

answers.text: AdministratorAccess always overrides SCPs
The CLI is broken whenever SCPs exist
The SCP limits the maximum permissions available in the account
Internet gateways can be created only by the management account

explanations.a: SCP denies remain effective for member accounts.
explanations.b: The authorization decision is working as designed.
explanations.c: AdministratorAccess in an identity policy cannot allow an action that an applicable SCP denies.
explanations.d: Member accounts can create internet gateways unless policies block them.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.1: Design and implement service control policies and organization-level guardrails.
questions.text: An SCP blocks a deployment pipeline unexpectedly after rollout. What should the security team do?

answers.text: Delete every SCP permanently
Grant root credentials to the pipeline
Ignore the failure because SCPs are unrelated to operations
Review denied actions in CloudTrail and test SCP changes in a lower-risk OU before broader enforcement

explanations.a: Removing all guardrails eliminates organization-level protection.
explanations.b: Root credentials do not bypass applicable SCP denies.
explanations.c: SCPs directly affect deployment authorization.
explanations.d: SCP guardrails should be validated with real deployment paths to avoid unplanned service disruption.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.1: Design and implement service control policies and organization-level guardrails.
questions.text: A company wants to prohibit creation of IAM users in workload accounts where federation is mandatory. What SCP fits?

answers.text: Deny IAM user and login profile creation in the workload OUs
A reminder in onboarding documentation only
A security group rule blocking port 443
A CloudWatch alarm on EC2 CPU

explanations.a: An SCP can enforce the workforce identity model by preventing local long-term human identities.
explanations.b: Documentation does not enforce the prohibition.
explanations.c: Network rules do not control IAM user creation.
explanations.d: CPU metrics do not prevent IAM user creation.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.1: Design and implement service control policies and organization-level guardrails.
questions.text: An SCP denies changing S3 Block Public Access, but central security automation must set the baseline. What is needed?

answers.text: Remove the SCP for every account during onboarding
A scoped exception for the approved central security role
Allow every principal to bypass the deny from the console
Use bucket names as the exception authority

explanations.a: Broad removal creates a governance gap.
explanations.b: Guardrails often need carefully defined exceptions for trusted baseline automation.
explanations.c: Console usage does not prove the action is approved.
explanations.d: Names do not authenticate the automation principal.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.1: Design and implement service control policies and organization-level guardrails.
questions.text: An organization wants to enforce tag requirements for cost and security ownership. What should be considered?

answers.text: Use only a spreadsheet of required tags
Deny all tag operations to every principal
SCPs with tag condition keys for supported create actions, plus Config detection for coverage gaps
Assume every AWS service supports identical tag conditions

explanations.a: A spreadsheet does not enforce or detect tag drift.
explanations.b: Blocking all tag operations can prevent required ownership metadata.
explanations.c: SCP tag conditions can prevent some untagged creation, and detection covers services or paths that cannot be fully prevented.
explanations.d: Tag enforcement support varies by service and action.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.1: Design and implement service control policies and organization-level guardrails.
questions.text: A security team wants to manage SCPs safely across many OUs. What operational practice matters most?

answers.text: Edit SCPs directly in production with no review
Apply new denies to every OU at once
Hide SCP changes from audit logs
Version-control policies, simulate impact, stage rollout, and monitor AccessDenied events

explanations.a: Unreviewed changes can disrupt critical workloads.
explanations.b: All-at-once rollout increases blast radius.
explanations.c: Policy changes should be auditable.
explanations.d: Organization guardrails can cause broad impact, so safe deployment and monitoring are essential.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A developer can create Lambda functions and pass any IAM role. What risk does this create?

answers.text: Privilege escalation through iam:PassRole to a more privileged execution role
Lower Lambda memory usage
Automatic deletion of CloudTrail logs
S3 object compression

explanations.a: PassRole allows a service to use a role, so broad PassRole can let users indirectly gain powerful permissions.
explanations.b: PassRole affects authorization, not memory allocation.
explanations.c: Broad PassRole does not itself delete logs unless the passed role enables actions that do so.
explanations.d: PassRole has no relationship to object compression.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A deployment role should pass only approved ECS task roles. What policy condition helps?

answers.text: Allow iam:PassRole on * with no conditions
Restrict iam:PassRole resources and use iam:PassedToService for ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com
Use only a role name prefix with no resource restriction
Grant PassRole through a security group rule

explanations.a: Broad PassRole increases privilege escalation risk.
explanations.b: PassRole should scope both the roles and the service that can receive them.
explanations.c: Names alone are weaker than resource and service constraints.
explanations.d: Security groups do not authorize IAM actions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A service-linked role is required by an AWS service. What should administrators understand?

answers.text: Service-linked roles are shared passwords for humans
Service-linked roles should always be edited to AdministratorAccess
The service-linked role is predefined for that service and should be created and used only as required by the service
Service-linked roles replace all resource policies

explanations.a: They are IAM roles for AWS services, not human credentials.
explanations.b: Their permissions are service-defined and should not be broadened arbitrarily.
explanations.c: Service-linked roles let AWS services perform actions on behalf of the account with service-defined trust and permissions.
explanations.d: Resource policies may still be required for specific services and access paths.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A user can create roles, attach policies, and pass those roles to EC2. What combination should be reviewed?

answers.text: Only the user's console theme
Only CloudFront cache TTL
Only the number of VPC endpoints
Role creation permissions, policy attachment permissions, and PassRole scope

explanations.a: Console preferences have no authorization effect.
explanations.b: Cache TTL does not control IAM role escalation paths.
explanations.c: Endpoint count does not explain role creation and PassRole risk.
explanations.d: Privilege escalation can occur when a principal can create or modify a role and then pass it to a service.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A Lambda function needs to access a VPC resource. Which role relationship matters?

answers.text: The Lambda execution role must have permissions for required service actions, including VPC ENI management when needed
A human IAM group must be attached to the function
The function must use root credentials to create network interfaces
A bucket ACL must authorize ENI creation

explanations.a: AWS services use execution roles to perform actions required by the workload configuration and runtime.
explanations.b: IAM groups are not function execution identities.
explanations.c: Root credentials are inappropriate for Lambda service operations.
explanations.d: Bucket ACLs do not grant EC2 network interface permissions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A security team wants to prevent users from passing security-admin roles to CloudFormation. What policy control is appropriate?

answers.text: Allow all PassRole actions during business hours
Deny iam:PassRole for privileged roles except approved deployment automation
Hide privileged role names from users but allow PassRole
Delete CloudFormation to avoid role passing

explanations.a: Time alone does not ensure safe role passing.
explanations.b: High-privilege roles should not be passable by general users or untrusted services.
explanations.c: Obscurity does not prevent API use when permissions allow it.
explanations.d: The service can be used safely with scoped roles and controls.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A service-linked role was deleted and a service stopped working. What is the proper response?

answers.text: Replace it with the account root user credentials
Create a random role with the same display name but different trust
Recreate the service-linked role through the service or IAM process and review why deletion was allowed
Disable CloudTrail so deletion is not visible

explanations.a: Root credentials are not a service-linked role replacement.
explanations.b: Trust and permissions must match the service-linked role requirements.
explanations.c: Some AWS services require their service-linked roles for operations, and deletion controls should be reviewed.
explanations.d: Audit visibility should remain enabled.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.2: Design and implement secure cross-service access with PassRole and service-linked roles.
questions.text: A CI/CD role needs PassRole for deployment but not for every role in the account. What is the best design?

answers.text: Grant PassRole on all roles because deployment is automated
Let developers choose any role at deployment time with no review
Use application environment names as the only enforcement
Create a path or tag convention for deployable roles and restrict PassRole to that approved set

explanations.a: Automation can still be compromised or misconfigured.
explanations.b: Unreviewed role selection can introduce privilege escalation.
explanations.c: Environment names do not enforce PassRole authorization by themselves.
explanations.d: A governed role set lets pipelines deploy workloads without passing unrelated privileged roles.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: A SaaS vendor needs to list CloudWatch metrics in a customer account. Which access model should be used?

answers.text: Cross-account role with external ID and least-privilege read permissions
An administrator access key emailed to the vendor
Public access to every CloudWatch dashboard
A shared root password entered in the vendor portal

explanations.a: Third-party integrations should use scoped temporary access and external ID protection against confused deputy risks.
explanations.b: Long-term administrator keys expose excessive privileges.
explanations.c: Public dashboards are not a controlled API integration.
explanations.d: Root credential sharing is unsafe and unnecessary.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: An application in Account A cannot read a secret in Account B. The secret policy trusts the role, but decrypt fails. What should be checked?

answers.text: Only the secret description length
The KMS key policy and IAM permissions for the role
Only the source VPC CIDR
Only CloudFront geolocation settings

explanations.a: Description length does not authorize decrypt.
explanations.b: Cross-account secret retrieval requires both secret access and KMS decrypt authorization.
explanations.c: Network range does not grant KMS permission.
explanations.d: Geolocation does not authorize Secrets Manager retrieval.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: A service integration fails because the source service is not allowed to publish to an SQS queue. What should be reviewed?

answers.text: Only the queue visibility timeout
Only the message body schema
The SQS resource policy, source ARN condition, and service principal
Only the producer's dashboard widgets

explanations.a: Visibility timeout affects consumers and not send authorization.
explanations.b: Message schema does not grant SendMessage permission.
explanations.c: Service-to-service SQS delivery depends on a queue policy that trusts the correct service and source.
explanations.d: Dashboards do not authorize service integration.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: A third-party OIDC provider integration fails role assumption. What should be validated?

answers.text: Only the EC2 instance family
Only S3 bucket storage class
Only the user's browser zoom level
OIDC provider thumbprint or configuration, token audience, subject conditions, and role trust policy

explanations.a: Instance family does not validate OIDC trust.
explanations.b: Storage class has no relationship to OIDC role assumption.
explanations.c: Browser settings do not affect token trust evaluation.
explanations.d: OIDC federation relies on trusted token claims that match the role trust conditions.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: An application uses Cognito user identities and must access AWS resources with scoped permissions. Which pattern fits?

answers.text: Use Cognito identity pools or application backend role assumption with scoped IAM roles
Put AWS administrator keys in the mobile app
Use one unauthenticated role for all sensitive actions
Grant access based only on the app icon

explanations.a: Application identities need a controlled bridge to AWS permissions rather than broad static credentials.
explanations.b: Client-side administrator keys can be extracted and abused.
explanations.c: Unauthenticated broad access exposes backend resources.
explanations.d: Application branding does not authorize AWS requests.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: A CloudWatch Logs subscription to a cross-account Kinesis stream is failing. What should be checked?

answers.text: Only the stream shard naming style
Destination policy, IAM role permissions, KMS key policy if encrypted, and source log group configuration
Only Route 53 TTL
Only the application code language

explanations.a: Shard names do not grant cross-account delivery.
explanations.b: Cross-account log delivery requires destination trust, write permissions, encryption permissions, and correct subscription setup.
explanations.c: DNS TTL does not authorize log subscriptions.
explanations.d: Programming language does not authorize CloudWatch Logs delivery.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: An external security scanner needs temporary read-only access during assessments. What access lifecycle is appropriate?

answers.text: Permanent administrator access for all future assessments
A public resource policy on every asset to scan
Time-bound role access with narrow permissions, external ID where applicable, and audit monitoring
A shared access key reused by all vendors

explanations.a: Permanent broad access is unnecessary and risky.
explanations.b: Public access is not a safe assessment mechanism.
explanations.c: Temporary scoped access reduces exposure and supports assessment accountability.
explanations.d: Shared keys reduce attribution and are hard to rotate.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.3: Design and troubleshoot IAM access for AWS services, applications, and third-party integrations.
questions.text: A service denies access even though the application role has an allow. What troubleshooting path should be used?

answers.text: Check only whether the role name looks correct
Change the application port number first
Delete unrelated alarms
Review identity policy, resource policy, SCPs, boundaries, session policies, KMS policies, and service-specific conditions

explanations.a: Names do not prove effective permissions.
explanations.b: Network ports do not resolve IAM authorization failures.
explanations.c: Alarms do not grant service access.
explanations.d: Service access failures often involve multiple policy layers and conditions beyond the immediate role policy.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: A security team wants alerts when privileged roles are assumed. Which events should be monitored?

answers.text: CloudTrail AssumeRole events for the privileged role ARNs with session context
Only EC2 CPU utilization events
Only S3 object size changes
Only CloudFront cache hit ratio

explanations.a: Role assumption events show who obtained privileged temporary credentials and from where.
explanations.b: CPU metrics do not show identity activity.
explanations.c: Object sizes do not identify privileged role assumption.
explanations.d: Cache ratio does not audit IAM activity.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: A root user was used in a member account. What should the monitoring workflow do?

answers.text: Ignore root activity if no CPU alarm fired
Alert security, review CloudTrail activity, confirm MFA, and validate whether the use was approved
Delete the root activity event
Grant root credentials to more responders

explanations.a: CPU state does not determine identity risk.
explanations.b: Root activity is high risk and should trigger immediate review and evidence capture.
explanations.c: Audit events should be preserved.
explanations.d: Broader root access increases risk.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: A policy was changed to allow public access to a sensitive bucket. Which audit sources help identify the actor?

answers.text: Only VPC Flow Logs
Only KMS key rotation schedule
CloudTrail events for PutBucketPolicy or related changes and identity session context
Only the bucket object count

explanations.a: Flow logs show network metadata and not bucket policy management calls.
explanations.b: Rotation schedule does not show who changed a bucket policy.
explanations.c: CloudTrail records S3 policy management API calls and the principal context.
explanations.d: Object count does not identify the policy actor.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: An administrator creates a new IAM access key for a dormant user. What monitoring should exist?

answers.text: Only a cost alarm for monthly spend
Only application latency dashboards
Only a manual review at the end of the year
EventBridge or Security Hub workflow for CreateAccessKey events on high-risk or dormant identities

explanations.a: Cost alarms can detect financial anomalies but not key creation by identity.
explanations.b: Latency does not audit IAM credential creation.
explanations.c: Annual review is too delayed for credential persistence risk.
explanations.d: New long-term credentials for dormant or privileged identities can indicate persistence and should be investigated.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: A security engineer needs to validate that no external accounts can access critical resources. Which service helps?

answers.text: IAM Access Analyzer
Amazon EFS throughput mode
AWS Backup copy jobs
CloudFront origin shield

explanations.a: Access Analyzer evaluates resource policies for access outside the defined zone of trust.
explanations.b: Throughput mode does not analyze access policies.
explanations.c: Backup copy does not detect external resource access.
explanations.d: Origin Shield does not evaluate IAM trust boundaries.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: A company wants a periodic report of unused IAM permissions. Which evidence helps?

answers.text: Only role creation dates
Service last accessed data and Access Analyzer policy recommendations
Only the number of tags on a role
Only dashboard refresh intervals

explanations.a: Creation date does not show which actions are used.
explanations.b: Usage information can identify permissions that can be removed or reduced.
explanations.c: Tag count does not reveal unused permissions.
explanations.d: Refresh intervals do not analyze IAM usage.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: An unexpected AssumeRole event comes from a new external IP. What should be correlated?

answers.text: Only unrelated EBS volume metrics
Only Route 53 domain registration contacts
Identity provider logs, CloudTrail sourceIPAddress, session name, MFA context, and subsequent API actions
Only the SQS queue retention period

explanations.a: Volume metrics do not validate role assumption.
explanations.b: Registration contacts do not explain the session.
explanations.c: Note that Identity activity auditing requires linking authentication context with AWS session behavior.
explanations.d: Queue retention does not identify session activity.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.4: Monitor, audit, and validate identity activity and access changes.
questions.text: A permission set was modified in IAM Identity Center. What audit evidence should be captured?

answers.text: Only a screenshot after the change
Only the account billing report
Only the number of groups in the identity provider
CloudTrail events, administrator identity, change request, before-and-after permission set definition, and affected assignments

explanations.a: A final screenshot lacks actor, approval, and before-state context.
explanations.b: Billing reports do not audit permission set changes.
explanations.c: Group count does not show what permission set changed.
explanations.d: Access change validation needs actor, approval, policy delta, and scope of users or accounts affected.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A company wants to eliminate long-term access keys for human administrators. What should it use?

answers.text: Federated access with MFA and temporary role sessions
Permanent administrator keys stored on laptops
A shared IAM user for all administrators
Root access keys rotated annually

explanations.a: Federation with MFA avoids persistent keys and supports auditable temporary access.
explanations.b: Long-term administrator keys are high-risk credentials.
explanations.c: Shared users remove individual accountability.
explanations.d: Root access keys should not be used for routine administration.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A break-glass role exists for emergencies. What controls should apply?

answers.text: No logging to protect responder privacy
MFA requirement, narrow trust, short session duration, alerting, and post-use review
Permanent assignment to every employee
A shared password posted in the incident channel

explanations.a: Break-glass use needs strong audit evidence.
explanations.b: Emergency access must be available but tightly monitored and time-limited.
explanations.c: Broad permanent emergency access increases risk.
explanations.d: Shared passwords are unsafe and not auditable.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: An IAM user access key has not been used for 180 days. What lifecycle action is appropriate?

answers.text: Increase the key's permissions to test it
Publish the key ID and secret for ownership discovery
Disable or remove the key after owner validation and change control
Ignore unused keys forever

explanations.a: Testing by broadening access creates unnecessary risk.
explanations.b: Secrets must not be exposed.
explanations.c: Stale long-term credentials increase risk and should be retired through a controlled process.
explanations.d: Unused keys can be compromised later and should be managed.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A production role has a 12-hour session duration for high-privilege access. What should be considered?

answers.text: Set session duration to unlimited
Disable MFA to reduce friction
Use shared sessions for all responders
Reduce session duration based on operational need and require reauthentication for privileged use

explanations.a: Unlimited sessions would increase exposure.
explanations.b: Privileged access should use stronger authentication.
explanations.c: Shared sessions reduce accountability.
explanations.d: Shorter privileged sessions limit the window of misuse if credentials are compromised.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A credential rotation policy applies to database secrets used by workloads. What must applications support?

answers.text: Retrieving current secret versions and refreshing cached credentials safely
Hardcoding the first password in source code
Printing every new secret in logs
Disabling authentication during rotation

explanations.a: Rotation is effective only when applications can use updated credentials without prolonged stale caching.
explanations.b: Hardcoded secrets cannot rotate safely.
explanations.c: It logs must not expose rotated secret values.
explanations.d: Authentication should remain enforced during rotation.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A company wants to detect console sign-ins without MFA for sensitive roles. What should be monitored?

answers.text: Only network packet size
CloudTrail sign-in and role assumption events with MFA context and privileged role identifiers
Only S3 lifecycle transitions
Only application feature flag changes

explanations.a: Packet size does not show MFA state.
explanations.b: MFA compliance for privileged access requires identity events that include authentication context.
explanations.c: Object lifecycle does not identify sign-in authentication factors.
explanations.d: Feature flags do not prove MFA usage.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A root user has no MFA device configured in a newly created account. What should be done?

answers.text: Share the root password with every administrator
Create root access keys for automation
Enable MFA on the root user and restrict routine root use
Disable CloudTrail because root is trusted

explanations.a: Sharing root credentials creates severe accountability and compromise risk.
explanations.b: Root access keys should not be used for automation.
explanations.c: Root credentials are highly privileged and should be protected with MFA and used only for tasks requiring root.
explanations.d: Root activity must be auditable.

questions.name: Identity and Access Management
questions.objective: Skill 4.3.5: Manage credential lifecycle, MFA, session duration, and emergency access.
questions.text: A developer accidentally committed an AWS access key to a repository. What response is required?

answers.text: Leave the key active until the next scheduled rotation
Only rename the IAM user
Post the key in a ticket so others can test it
Disable or rotate the key, investigate CloudTrail activity, remove the secret from repository history where possible, and update controls

explanations.a: Delay gives attackers more time to use the key.
explanations.b: Renaming does not invalidate the exposed key.
explanations.c: Further sharing increases exposure.
explanations.d: Exposed credentials require immediate containment, usage review, and prevention improvements.
